seoTitle: Free HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 Frame Inspector
metaDescription: Decode hex dumps of HTTP/2 frames with SETTINGS, HEADERS, DATA and GOAWAY, or HTTP/3 frames with varints. Free, runs in your browser.
intro: Paste a hex dump of HTTP/2 frames, with or without the client preface, or HTTP/3 frames, and see each frame decoded: type, flags, stream and length, including SETTINGS, HEADERS, DATA and GOAWAY.
why:
HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 are binary, so when a proxy, a test client or a hand-built server misbehaves, you cannot read the traffic as text. A captured hex dump is accurate but impenetrable: you have to read nine-byte frame headers, track stream IDs and decode flags by eye, and HTTP/3 uses variable-length integers on top.

This inspector splits the dump into frames and explains each one. HPACK header blocks are shown with their fields where possible, but Huffman-coded strings are shown as hex and QPACK blocks are not decoded, so you still need a full tool for header contents. It is meant for learning and debugging protocol-level issues. The decoding runs in your browser and your capture is not uploaded.
howTo: Paste the hex dump of the frames, with or without spaces.
Read the decoded frames in order, with type, flags, stream ID and payload details.
Compare them with the expected behaviour in the RFC to find the unexpected frame or setting.

faq.q: Why are some header strings shown as hex?
faq.a: HPACK can compress strings with a Huffman code, and this tool shows those strings as hex instead of decoding them. QPACK blocks in HTTP/3 are not decoded either, so header content is limited.

faq.q: Does it need the connection preface?
faq.a: For HTTP/2 the client preface is recognised if present, but you can also paste only the frames. The decoder reads the frame headers from the start of what you paste.

faq.q: Can I analyse encrypted traffic with it?
faq.a: No. You need the decrypted frames, for example from a debug log or a capture decrypted with a key log file. Raw TLS records on the wire will not decode as frames.
